name: Athletic Training
description: Introduces the profession of athletic training, covering injury prevention, evaluation, first aid, taping, rehabilitation, and career pathways. Students gain hands-on knowledge of caring for the physically active.

modules.title: Introduction to Athletic Training
modules.objectives: Define athletic training as a healthcare profession; describe the certified athletic trainer (ATC) role; identify diverse work settings.
modules.readingNote: NATA — scope, settings, education, and healthcare role of athletic trainers (ATs).
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson and teacher-reviewed course materials for the athletic-training profession overview.
modules.assignment: Create a career-and-scope brief for a fictional high school deciding whether to hire an athletic trainer (AT). Use the NATA reading and module lesson to list five AT responsibilities, three work settings, the current education/certification pathway, and two differences between an AT and a personal trainer. Submit: a one-page brief plus a 150-word recommendation. Include source links and label any fact that depends on state regulation. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: accurate professional terminology, current pathway, scope boundaries, evidence from the reading, and a recommendation that does not authorize unqualified practice.

modules.title: Anatomy for Athletic Trainers
modules.objectives: Identify major bones, joints, muscles, and ligaments relevant to sport injury; use correct anatomical terminology for location and movement. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: Musculoskeletal Anatomy Review — for a visual explanation of Anatomy for Athletic Trainers before guided practice
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Draw a neutral-position body outline or use a teacher-supplied blank outline, then label 20 items: at least five bones, five muscles or tendons, five ligaments or joint structures, and five directional or movement terms. Correct these four fictional statements: (1) a tendon connects bone to bone; (2) the ankle is proximal to the knee; (3) dorsiflexion points the toes downward; and (4) the quadriceps lie on the posterior lower leg. Submit: the labeled diagram plus a four-row correction table. Include: each incorrect statement, its correction, and a one-sentence anatomical explanation. Evaluation: anatomical accuracy, readable labels, correct location and movement language, and evidence-based explanations for all four corrections.

modules.title: Injury Prevention Strategies
modules.objectives: Identify intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors for sport injury; explain how warm-up, conditioning, protective equipment, and rule enforcement reduce risk.
modules.readingNote: NIAMS — acute and chronic sports injuries, risk factors, prevention, and when professional evaluation is needed.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Design an injury-prevention plan for a fictional 12-week school soccer season. The case supplies: two athletes with prior ankle sprain, a sudden proposed 40% workload increase, poor field lighting, and inconsistent warm-up. Submit: a risk table separating intrinsic and extrinsic factors, a progressive-load plan, a 10-minute warm-up outline, equipment/environment checks, and three stop-or-refer criteria. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: risks tied to specific controls, gradual progression and recovery, feasible monitoring, and no promise that injury can be eliminated.

modules.title: First Aid and Emergency Procedures
modules.objectives: Describe Emergency Action Plan (EAP) components; demonstrate first aid for common on-field emergencies; explain criteria for activating EMS.
modules.readingNote: American Red Cross — first-aid education and training pathways; course work does not substitute for certification.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — complete the module tabletop Emergency Action Plan scenario; this practice does not provide first-aid certification.
modules.assignment: Draft an Emergency Action Plan for a fictional high school basketball event. The scenario provides one gym entrance, an AED at the main office, spotty cell reception, and four available staff roles. Submit: a one-page EAP with venue address/access route, role assignments, communication backup, EMS activation criteria, emergency-equipment locations, and post-event documentation; add a tabletop script for sudden cardiac arrest and suspected spinal injury. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: clear chain of command, rapid AED/EMS access, safe non-movement boundary, communication redundancy, and no procedure beyond the responder's training.

modules.title: Taping and Bracing Techniques
modules.objectives: Explain purposes of prophylactic taping and bracing; describe ankle and wrist taping procedures; distinguish functional from prophylactic braces.
modules.readingNote: GIIS module lesson — taping and bracing concepts; hands-on application requires qualified supervision.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: NSCA — Sports Medicine Techniques — for independent practice on Taping and Bracing Techniques before submitting the assignment
modules.assignment: Create a decision guide for four fictional situations: (A) an athlete with a recurrent lateral ankle sprain who has completed rehabilitation and is cleared for practice; (B) an athlete with acute swelling and visible deformity after a new injury; (C) an athlete with impaired foot sensation and a known adhesive allergy; and (D) an uninjured athlete with no instability history during routine training. Compare prophylactic tape, a lace-up brace, a rigid functional brace, and no external support. Submit: one document containing a four-row comparison table and an ankle-taping sequence drawn on paper or slides with annotation labels; do not tape a person unless a qualified instructor directly supervises. Include: evidence from the assigned reading or module lesson to justify each choice, intended motion control, skin and circulation checks, contraindications or referral needs, and why external support never replaces rehabilitation or medical evaluation. Evaluation: accurate purpose, safe checks, logical and evidence-based equipment choice, correct referral decisions, and explicit scope limits.

modules.title: Rehabilitation Principles
modules.objectives: Describe phases of injury rehabilitation; explain PRICE protocol and progressive loading; identify evidence-based return-to-play criteria. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: NIAMS — recovery principles and the role of professional evaluation for sports injuries.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional Grade II lateral ankle sprain case: moderate swelling, partial ligament injury, pain with weight bearing, and no fracture red flags after professional evaluation. Build a four-phase rehabilitation plan with goals, example exercises, dosage ranges, progression/regression criteria, and objective return-to-participation measures for pain, swelling, range of motion, strength, balance, and sport tasks. Submit: a phase table plus 200-word rationale. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: criterion-based progression, appropriate load management, measurable outcomes, and medical clearance boundary.

modules.title: Common Sports Injuries
modules.objectives: Identify mechanism, signs, symptoms, and initial management of the most common sport injuries by body region. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson and teacher-reviewed course materials for common sports-injury recognition and referral boundaries.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Create a field reference card for five fictional injuries: lateral ankle sprain, hamstring strain, suspected fracture, overuse stress injury, and shoulder instability. For each, list likely mechanism, observable signs/symptoms, immediate actions within a student aide's scope, red flags, and referral urgency. Submit: a one-page table plus two short compare/contrast notes (sprain vs strain; acute vs chronic). Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: accurate distinctions, safe escalation, concise field usability, and no diagnosis or return-to-play decision by an unqualified student.

modules.title: Concussion Management
modules.objectives: Define concussion; identify signs and symptoms; explain CDC Heads Up protocols and the graduated return-to-play and return-to-learn protocol.
modules.readingNote: CDC HEADS UP — immediate response to suspected concussion and medical-evaluation boundary.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: CDC Heads Up — Coaches Concussion Training
modules.assignment: Use the CDC HEADS UP reading to write a school concussion-response protocol. Include recognition signs, immediate removal from play, emergency danger signs, medical evaluation, return-to-learn supports, and a graduated return-to-sport sequence controlled by a healthcare professional. Apply it to a fictional athlete whose headache returns during step three. Submit: protocol flowchart plus a 200-word case response. Include: every requested table, visual, or written component; specific evidence from the fictional case or assigned reading; the named course concepts; and the reasoning, limitations, or safety boundaries stated above. Evaluation: no same-day return, correct symptom-response step, coordinated school/family communication, and clear healthcare clearance authority.

quizQuestions.question: The professional credential for a certified athletic trainer is:
quizQuestions.answer: ATC
quizQuestions.explanation: ATC (Athletic Trainer Certified) is awarded by the Board of Certification to qualified athletic trainers.

quizQuestions.question: Athletic trainers primarily work with:
options: Physically active individuals across all ages and settings
quizQuestions.answer: Physically active individuals across all ages and settings
quizQuestions.explanation: Certified athletic trainers work in high schools, colleges, professional sports, military, clinics, and performing arts.

quizQuestions.question: Which activity falls within the athletic trainer’s healthcare role?
options: Preventing, evaluating, and rehabilitating injuries within professional scope
quizQuestions.answer: Preventing, evaluating, and rehabilitating injuries within professional scope
quizQuestions.explanation: Athletic trainers are healthcare professionals whose work includes risk reduction, clinical evaluation, emergency care, treatment, and rehabilitation within regulation and collaboration requirements.

quizQuestions.question: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is located in the:
quizQuestions.answer: Knee
quizQuestions.explanation: The ACL is a major stabilizing ligament inside the knee joint, connecting femur to tibia.

quizQuestions.question: A sprain involves injury to:
quizQuestions.answer: A ligament
quizQuestions.explanation: Sprains are ligament injuries (bone-to-bone), while strains involve muscles or tendons.

quizQuestions.question: The rotator cuff is a group of muscles and tendons surrounding the:
quizQuestions.answer: Shoulder joint
quizQuestions.explanation: The rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) stabilizes the glenohumeral joint.

quizQuestions.question: Which directional term means closer to the body’s midline?
quizQuestions.answer: Medial
quizQuestions.explanation: Medial means toward the midline; lateral means away from it, distal means farther from an attachment point, and posterior means toward the back.

quizQuestions.question: Intrinsic risk factors for sport injury include:
options: Previous injury history and muscle imbalances
quizQuestions.answer: Previous injury history and muscle imbalances
quizQuestions.explanation: Intrinsic factors are internal athlete characteristics influencing injury susceptibility. It connects the correct answer to Injury Prevention Strategies and separates it from plausible distractors.

quizQuestions.question: Neuromuscular training programs like FIFA 11+ primarily prevent:
quizQuestions.answer: ACL injuries
quizQuestions.explanation: FIFA 11+ and similar programs target landing mechanics and hip/core strength to reduce ACL injury rates.

quizQuestions.question: The most effective prevention strategy for overuse injuries is:
options: Gradually increasing training load with adequate recovery
quizQuestions.answer: Gradually increasing training load with adequate recovery
quizQuestions.explanation: Overuse injuries result from repetitive microtrauma exceeding tissue repair; progressive load management prevents them.

quizQuestions.question: The primary goal of an Emergency Action Plan (EAP) is to:
options: Ensure rapid, coordinated response to athletic emergencies
quizQuestions.answer: Ensure rapid, coordinated response to athletic emergencies
quizQuestions.explanation: An EAP outlines roles, communication, and equipment to enable a fast, organized emergency response.

quizQuestions.question: Which finding is most characteristic of exertional heat stroke?
options: Mild muscle soreness with normal thinking
Central nervous system dysfunction with severe heat illness
A cool athlete who is fully alert
quizQuestions.answer: Central nervous system dysfunction with severe heat illness
quizQuestions.explanation: Altered mental status or other central nervous system dysfunction in severe heat illness is an emergency; activate the emergency plan and begin rapid cooling according to trained protocol.

quizQuestions.question: Recommended first aid for a suspected spinal injury is:
options: Have the athlete walk off the field
Stabilize the head and neck; do not move the athlete
Apply ice and return to play
quizQuestions.answer: Stabilize the head and neck; do not move the athlete
quizQuestions.explanation: Suspected spinal injuries require immobilization — movement without proper precautions risks permanent paralysis.

quizQuestions.question: In First Aid and Emergency Procedures, AED stands for:
quizQuestions.answer: Automated External Defibrillator
quizQuestions.explanation: An AED delivers an electrical shock to restore normal heart rhythm during sudden cardiac arrest.

quizQuestions.question: Prophylactic ankle taping primarily prevents:
options: Ankle sprains by limiting excessive inversion
quizQuestions.answer: Ankle sprains by limiting excessive inversion
quizQuestions.explanation: Prophylactic taping restricts excessive inversion motion, preventing lateral ankle sprains.

quizQuestions.question: Pre-wrap is applied before athletic tape to:
quizQuestions.answer: Protect skin from adhesive
quizQuestions.explanation: Pre-wrap creates a protective barrier between the skin and rigid athletic tape.

quizQuestions.question: What is a key advantage of a reusable ankle brace compared with single-use taping?
options: It guarantees prevention of every sprain
It can provide repeatable support and be reapplied, though fit and skin checks remain necessary
It eliminates the need for rehabilitation
It should be worn over an acute fracture without evaluation
quizQuestions.answer: It can provide repeatable support and be reapplied, though fit and skin checks remain necessary
quizQuestions.explanation: A properly fitted brace can offer consistent, reusable support, but it still requires circulation/skin checks and does not replace evaluation or rehabilitation.

quizQuestions.question: After taping or bracing, which check is essential before activity?
options: Confirm the support is as tight as possible
Check comfort, sensation, color, temperature, and circulation distal to the support
Ask only whether the athlete likes its appearance
Cover any new numbness with more tape
quizQuestions.answer: Check comfort, sensation, color, temperature, and circulation distal to the support
quizQuestions.explanation: Numbness, color or temperature change, unusual pain, or impaired circulation requires loosening/removing the support and reassessment.

quizQuestions.question: The acute inflammatory phase of injury healing lasts approximately:
quizQuestions.answer: 0–72 hours post-injury
quizQuestions.explanation: Acute inflammation begins immediately after injury and typically resolves within 72 hours.

quizQuestions.question: During the proliferative phase of healing, the primary tissue deposited is:
quizQuestions.answer: Type III collagen (scar tissue)
quizQuestions.explanation: Fibroblasts lay down type III collagen forming immature scar tissue during the proliferative phase (days 3–21).

quizQuestions.question: Progressive loading in rehabilitation means:
options: Systematically increasing exercise demand as tissue heals
Avoiding all exercise until fully healed
quizQuestions.answer: Systematically increasing exercise demand as tissue heals
quizQuestions.explanation: Progressive loading stimulates tissue remodeling without exceeding the healing tissue's tolerance.

quizQuestions.question: Which return-to-participation decision is most defensible?
options: Time elapsed is the only criterion
The athlete meets objective pain, motion, strength, balance, and sport-task criteria and has required medical clearance
The athlete can tolerate pain medication
The athlete wants to play despite worsening swelling
quizQuestions.answer: The athlete meets objective pain, motion, strength, balance, and sport-task criteria and has required medical clearance
quizQuestions.explanation: Return decisions should be criterion-based and include functional testing and appropriate clinical clearance, not calendar time or pressure alone.

quizQuestions.question: A Grade II ankle sprain involves:
options: Partial ligament tear with moderate pain and swelling
Complete ligament rupture with severe instability
quizQuestions.answer: Partial ligament tear with moderate pain and swelling
quizQuestions.explanation: Grade II sprains involve partial ligament tearing with moderate pain, swelling, and some instability.

quizQuestions.question: A concussion is classified as:
quizQuestions.answer: A mild traumatic brain injury
quizQuestions.explanation: A concussion is a mild TBI caused by biomechanical forces that temporarily alter brain function.

quizQuestions.question: Which finding after a sports injury most clearly requires urgent referral?
options: Mild soreness that resolves with rest
Visible deformity or loss of distal circulation/sensation
A small bruise with full painless motion
quizQuestions.answer: Visible deformity or loss of distal circulation/sensation
quizQuestions.explanation: Deformity or neurovascular compromise can indicate serious injury and requires emergency evaluation rather than routine sideline management.

quizQuestions.question: Concussion is diagnosed primarily by:
options: Clinical evaluation of signs and symptoms
quizQuestions.answer: Clinical evaluation of signs and symptoms
quizQuestions.explanation: Standard neuroimaging appears normal in most concussions; diagnosis is clinical.

quizQuestions.question: CDC's 'When in Doubt, Sit Them Out' means:
options: Rest only if the athlete loses consciousness
Remove any suspected concussion athlete from play immediately
Athletes may return after 15 minutes if symptoms resolve
quizQuestions.answer: Remove any suspected concussion athlete from play immediately
quizQuestions.explanation: The CDC recommends immediate removal to prevent second-impact syndrome. This reinforces the Concussion Management idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

quizQuestions.question: Second-impact syndrome occurs when:
options: An athlete sustains two concussions years apart
A second head injury occurs before full recovery from the first concussion
An athlete is concussed twice in the same game with no symptoms
quizQuestions.answer: A second head injury occurs before full recovery from the first concussion
quizQuestions.explanation: Second-impact syndrome can cause rapid, catastrophic brain swelling and is potentially fatal.

quizQuestions.question: If concussion symptoms return during a graduated return-to-sport step, the athlete should:
options: Advance to the next step to build tolerance
Stop activity, contact the healthcare provider, and resume only as directed after symptoms settle
Return to full competition the same day
Ignore symptoms if balance appears normal
quizQuestions.answer: Stop activity, contact the healthcare provider, and resume only as directed after symptoms settle
quizQuestions.explanation: CDC guidance calls for stopping when symptoms recur and involving the healthcare provider; progression resumes from an appropriate earlier step only after recovery guidance is met.

questions.question: Which credential identifies a certified athletic trainer in this course?
questions.answer: ATC
questions.explanation: ATC is awarded by the Board of Certification to qualified athletic trainers.

questions.question: A sprain is an injury to which type of tissue?
questions.answer: A ligament
questions.explanation: Sprains are ligament injuries; strains involve muscles or tendons. It connects the correct answer to Athletic Training midterm concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: In Athletic Training midterm concepts, The ACL is located in the:
questions.answer: Knee
questions.explanation: The anterior cruciate ligament is a major stabilizing ligament inside the knee joint.

questions.question: Which training habit best helps reduce overuse injury risk?
options: Gradually increasing load with adequate recovery
Repeating the same high-intensity workout daily
questions.answer: Gradually increasing load with adequate recovery
questions.explanation: Gradual progression and recovery help tissues adapt to training demands. Students need to recognize why Gradually increasing load with adequate recovery matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: In emergency response, what does AED stand for?
questions.answer: Automated External Defibrillator
questions.explanation: An AED delivers electrical shock to restore normal heart rhythm during cardiac arrest.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an athletic trainer (AT) from a personal trainer?
options: ATs provide regulated healthcare services; personal trainers primarily guide fitness and conditioning
The roles are identical in every state
Personal trainers diagnose injuries while ATs sell memberships
ATs never work outside competitive sports
questions.answer: ATs provide regulated healthcare services; personal trainers primarily guide fitness and conditioning
questions.explanation: ATs are healthcare professionals with accredited education, certification, and state-regulated practice; personal trainers focus primarily on fitness instruction.

questions.question: Moving a limb away from the body’s midline is called:
questions.answer: Abduction
questions.explanation: Abduction moves a body part away from the midline; adduction moves it toward the midline.

questions.question: Which is an extrinsic injury-risk factor?
questions.answer: Poorly maintained playing surface
questions.explanation: Extrinsic risks come from outside the athlete, such as environment, equipment, rules, or workload design.

questions.question: Why should training load increase gradually?
options: To allow tissue adaptation and reduce overload that exceeds recovery capacity
questions.answer: To allow tissue adaptation and reduce overload that exceeds recovery capacity
questions.explanation: Progressive load helps tissues adapt while avoiding abrupt spikes that can increase overuse-injury risk.

questions.question: What information belongs in a venue-specific Emergency Action Plan?
options: Address/access route, responder roles, communication method, and emergency-equipment locations
A promise that no emergency will occur
questions.answer: Address/access route, responder roles, communication method, and emergency-equipment locations
questions.explanation: An EAP must let responders locate the venue, activate help, assign roles, and retrieve needed equipment quickly.

questions.question: Which event requires immediate EMS activation?
options: An unresponsive athlete with absent or abnormal breathing
Delayed-onset soreness two days after exercise
questions.answer: An unresponsive athlete with absent or abnormal breathing
questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness with absent or abnormal breathing is a life-threatening emergency requiring EMS activation, CPR, and AED use by trained responders.

questions.question: Which response best fits suspected exertional heat stroke?
options: Delay action until a temperature reading is available
Activate the EAP and begin rapid whole-body cooling according to trained protocol
Give the athlete an energy drink and return them to play
questions.answer: Activate the EAP and begin rapid whole-body cooling according to trained protocol
questions.explanation: Severe heat illness with central nervous system dysfunction is an emergency; rapid cooling and EMS coordination are critical.

questions.question: In standard musculoskeletal injury terminology, which tissue is injured in a strain?
questions.answer: A muscle or tendon
questions.explanation: Strains involve muscle or tendon tissue, whereas sprains involve ligaments.

questions.question: Which prevention plan best addresses both intrinsic and extrinsic risks?
options: Ignore prior injury and replace the field
Use rehabilitation/neuromuscular training for prior injury and correct unsafe surfaces or equipment
Use braces for every athlete regardless of fit
Rely only on a pregame speech
questions.answer: Use rehabilitation/neuromuscular training for prior injury and correct unsafe surfaces or equipment
questions.explanation: A complete plan addresses athlete factors and environment/equipment factors with targeted controls.

questions.question: The Achilles tendon connects to the:
questions.answer: Calcaneus
questions.explanation: The Achilles tendon attaches the gastrocnemius and soleus to the heel bone.

questions.question: Which finding after taping means the support should be removed or adjusted immediately?
options: New numbness, color change, or increasing distal pain
The athlete requests a team color
questions.answer: New numbness, color change, or increasing distal pain
questions.explanation: Neurovascular symptoms after external support can indicate excessive compression and require prompt removal or adjustment and reassessment.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of prophylactic ankle taping or bracing?
options: Limit excessive motion associated with recurrent sprain risk
questions.answer: Limit excessive motion associated with recurrent sprain risk
questions.explanation: External support can limit risky motion, but it does not heal serious injury, eliminate risk, or replace rehabilitation.

questions.question: Second-impact syndrome can occur under which circumstance?
options: A second head injury occurs before full recovery from the first
An athlete is hit twice with no symptoms
questions.answer: A second head injury occurs before full recovery from the first
questions.explanation: Second-impact syndrome can cause rapid, catastrophic brain swelling and is potentially fatal.

questions.question: The rotator cuff surrounds the:
questions.answer: Shoulder
questions.explanation: The four rotator cuff muscles stabilize the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint. This reinforces the Athletic Training final concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: Compared with RICE, what additional step does PRICE add?
questions.answer: Protection
questions.explanation: PRICE adds protection to rest, ice, compression, and elevation. This reinforces the Athletic Training final concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: During rehabilitation, progression to a harder exercise should occur when:
options: The calendar reaches a preset date regardless of symptoms
The athlete meets defined criteria without an unacceptable increase in pain or swelling
questions.answer: The athlete meets defined criteria without an unacceptable increase in pain or swelling
questions.explanation: Criterion-based progression uses objective function and symptom response rather than time alone.

questions.question: Which description best fits a moderate Grade II ankle sprain?
options: Partial tear with moderate pain and swelling
questions.answer: Partial tear with moderate pain and swelling
questions.explanation: Grade II sprains involve partial tearing with moderate pain, swelling, and some instability.

questions.question: Which return-to-participation measure is most useful after a lower-extremity injury?
options: Pain-free walking as the only criterion
Pain-free range of motion, strength and balance comparison, and sport-specific task performance
The same calendar delay used for a previous athlete
One isolated strength result without symptom or task assessment
questions.answer: Pain-free range of motion, strength and balance comparison, and sport-specific task performance
questions.explanation: Return decisions rely on relevant clinical and functional measures plus required clearance, not unrelated characteristics.

questions.question: Which pattern most strongly suggests an overuse injury?
options: A sudden deformity after one collision
Pain that develops gradually with repeated loading and worsens over time
One brief muscle cramp that resolves
questions.answer: Pain that develops gradually with repeated loading and worsens over time
questions.explanation: Overuse injuries arise from repetitive load exceeding recovery and usually develop gradually rather than from one acute event.

questions.question: Graduated return to play after concussion requires:
options: Full contact return when symptoms resolve that day
Each step at least 24 hours apart, regression if symptoms return
questions.answer: Each step at least 24 hours apart, regression if symptoms return
questions.explanation: The graduated protocol ensures safe stepwise return to play. Students need to recognize why Each step at least 24 hours apart, regression if symptoms return matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: Stress fractures most commonly occur in:
questions.answer: Weight-bearing bones (tibia, metatarsals)
questions.explanation: Repetitive stress exceeding bone remodeling capacity causes stress fractures in weight-bearing bones.

questions.question: Why must concussion management include return-to-learn as well as return-to-sport?
options: Cognitive demands can worsen symptoms and may need temporary adjustment during recovery
Athletes should avoid school until every symptom disappears for a month
questions.answer: Cognitive demands can worsen symptoms and may need temporary adjustment during recovery
questions.explanation: Concussion can affect attention, memory, and symptom tolerance, so school supports should be individualized alongside medical management.

questions.question: Which injury mechanism does prophylactic ankle taping primarily try to limit?
questions.answer: Excessive inversion leading to sprains
questions.explanation: Ankle taping is commonly used to restrict excessive inversion, a common sprain mechanism.

questions.question: What is progressive loading in rehabilitation?
options: Increasing demand in planned steps as capacity improves
Keeping every exercise unchanged until discharge
Adding maximum resistance on day one
questions.answer: Increasing demand in planned steps as capacity improves
questions.explanation: Progressive loading challenges healing tissue within tolerance and advances only when response and function support it.

questions.question: Which finding after a suspected musculoskeletal injury is an emergency red flag?
options: Absent distal pulse or rapidly worsening loss of sensation
questions.answer: Absent distal pulse or rapidly worsening loss of sensation
questions.explanation: Loss of circulation or sensation can signal neurovascular compromise and requires urgent emergency evaluation.

questions.question: A Grade III ligament sprain generally involves:
options: A complete tear with substantial instability or loss of function
questions.answer: A complete tear with substantial instability or loss of function
questions.explanation: Grade III sprains are severe ligament disruptions and require professional evaluation and management.

questions.question: What should happen if swelling and pain increase after a rehabilitation session?
options: Reassess, reduce the load, and consult the supervising clinician as needed
Ignore the response if the plan is written
questions.answer: Reassess, reduce the load, and consult the supervising clinician as needed
questions.explanation: A worsening response suggests the current load exceeded tolerance and should trigger regression and clinical reassessment.

questions.question: Which action is appropriate for a student aide who suspects a serious injury?
options: Diagnose the injury and clear return to play
Protect the athlete, activate the plan, and notify the qualified healthcare professional
questions.answer: Protect the athlete, activate the plan, and notify the qualified healthcare professional
questions.explanation: A student should stay within scope, prevent further harm, and escalate to trained healthcare and emergency personnel.

questions.question: IT band syndrome most commonly affects:
questions.answer: Distance runners and cyclists
questions.explanation: Repetitive knee flexion-extension friction of the IT band over the lateral femoral condyle causes IT band syndrome.

questions.question: An athlete’s headache returns during step three of a graduated concussion return. What is the next action?
options: Stop activity and report the symptoms to the healthcare provider
Skip directly to competition after one hour
questions.answer: Stop activity and report the symptoms to the healthcare provider
questions.explanation: Symptom recurrence means the athlete is progressing too quickly; activity stops and the healthcare provider directs the next step.
